segments.name: The Bay, the Bank, and the Doctorate

stops.name: Minsk, the country the line comes from
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Wikipedia gives the Minsk area of present-day Belarus as the family's origin and gives no emigration date; the year shown is a placeholder for a generation and not a claim. Adleman himself is not attested at this coordinate.
stops.campa: The family are Jewish emigrants from the country around Minsk, in what is now Belarus. Nobody records the year they left or the port they sailed from. Adleman never stands here. The pin marks where the line that becomes him was living before it crossed an ocean, two generations before a boy is born in San Francisco and set to work on numbers. The year on this entry is a placeholder for a generation. No source supplies a real one, and the record keeps the blank instead of inventing a date.
suggested_refs: The Jewish communities of the Minsk gubernia before the emigration waves of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries

stops.name: San Francisco, the birth on the last day of the year
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (Wikipedia; MacTutor). The pin is the city; no source names the hospital or the quarter.
stops.campa: A son is born in San Francisco on the last day of 1945 to an appliance salesman and a bank teller. They name him Leonard Max Adleman. The family are Jewish, and the line behind them comes from the country around Minsk. No source names the hospital or the quarter of the city; the record holds the date exactly and the place only as a name. Half a century on, the arithmetic he helps assemble will stand under every transaction the banks of this city make, including the ones his mother once counted by hand at a teller's window.
suggested_refs: Standard biographical listings for Adleman give the city and the date and no further detail on the family's San Francisco address

stops.name: San Francisco, Hamlet in a high school classroom
stops.date_confidence: traditional. MacTutor preserves the episode without a year and without naming the school or the teacher; 1962 is a placeholder inside his high school years, and the month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: He calls himself, later, incredibly naive and immature, a boy with no ambition toward mathematics at all. An English teacher reads Hamlet aloud to the class, and by Adleman's own account the beauty of an idea reaches him for the first time through a play about a man who cannot decide. The same teacher tells him to go to Berkeley. No source names the teacher and no source names the school. What survives is the order of events, an English class before any mathematics, and one man's word for it decades later.
stops.quote: People think of mathematics as some kind of practical art, ... the point when you become a mathematician is where you somehow see through this and see the beauty and power of mathematics.
suggested_refs: MacTutor's account of the high school English teacher who read Hamlet and sent Adleman to Berkeley; the school is unnamed in all reachable sources

stops.name: Berkeley, the bachelor's degree in mathematics
stops.date_confidence: Degree and year attested (Wikipedia specifies a B.A. in mathematics; MacTutor gives 1968). Month and day are defaults. The research pool's 1963 enrollment year is unsourced and is not carried, and its 'BS' is corrected to B.A. The Sather Gate pin is corrected from 37.8716, which lands about 180 m north near Doe Library.
stops.campa: He arrives meaning to be a chemist, on the strength of a television program called Mr. Wizard. Fraternity brothers in Kappa Nu talk him toward medicine instead. He settles on mathematics and takes the degree in 1968, a B.A. out of the College of Letters and Science rather than the engineering school he will spend the rest of his working life inside. The gate he walks through is the one every Berkeley demonstration of those years forms up behind. No source says whether he stopped to listen.
suggested_refs: Berkeley commencement records for the College of Letters and Science, 1968

stops.name: 300 Montgomery Street, the programmer at Bank of America
stops.date_confidence: Employment attested (MacTutor); the month is a default. MacTutor names the employer and not the building, so the historic Bank of America headquarters stands in as a landmark and this pin is approximate.
stops.campa: The new graduate takes work as a computer programmer at Bank of America, writing for machines that keep ledgers. He is accepted to medical school during these years and turns it down. This is the only stretch of his life spent inside a commercial institution rather than a university, and the institution is a bank: exactly the kind of body that will, within twenty years, be unable to move a dollar without the cipher he has not yet helped to invent. No source names the branch or the floor.
suggested_refs: The Bank of America headquarters building at 300 Montgomery Street, used here as a landmark for an employer whose premises the sources do not specify

stops.name: San Francisco State, the physics that does not take
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor attests that he took classes at San Francisco State College while employed at the bank and that he quit; MacTutor gives no year, so 1969 is inference and the month and day are defaults. Coordinate corrected from the research pool's -122.4762, which lands about 330 m east of campus across 19th Avenue.
stops.campa: Still on the bank's payroll, he enrolls in physics at San Francisco State College and leaves quickly. The reason he gives is not difficulty. It is temperament: he wants to think about things rather than do things to them, and a laboratory is a place where you do things to them. Twenty-five years later he will spend months at a bench with pipettes and gels doing precisely what he refuses here, and that reversal produces the only experiment of his career.
stops.quote: I didn't like doing experiments, I liked thinking about things.
suggested_refs: San Francisco State College enrollment records for the late 1960s; no year is given in any reachable account

stops.name: Berkeley, the doctorate under Manuel Blum
stops.date_confidence: Year, thesis title and adviser attested (Mathematics Genealogy Project; MacTutor; Wikipedia). Month and day are defaults. The research pool pinned this to Evans Hall labelled EECS; Evans houses Mathematics and Statistics while EECS occupies Cory Hall, so no building is claimed and the campus coordinate is used instead.
stops.campa: He returns to Berkeley for a doctorate in electrical engineering and computer sciences under Manuel Blum, and submits Number Theoretic Aspects of Computational Complexity in 1976. The title already holds both halves of the later work: the theory of numbers on one side, the cost of computing on the other. His stated reason for taking the degree is not vocation. It is that a doctorate would further his career, which it does, in a direction nobody at the examination table could have named.
stops.quote: I thought that getting a PhD in computer science would at least further my career.
suggested_refs: Adleman, 'Number Theoretic Aspects of Computational Complexity', PhD thesis, University of California, Berkeley, 1976

segments.name: Cambridge: Breaking Codes One Through Forty-Two

stops.name: MIT, the office next to Rivest's
stops.date_confidence: Appointment year attested (MacTutor; ACM Turing Award citation); the month is a default for the academic year. The Building 2 pin follows the Mathematics Department address, and the specific office is not documented.
stops.campa: Adleman arrives at MIT as an assistant professor of mathematics, hired straight out of the doctorate to teach number theory. Ronald Rivest has the office beside his. Down the road at 545 Technology Square, in the Laboratory for Computer Science, Rivest and an Israeli visitor named Adi Shamir are working at a problem set the year before by Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman: a cipher whose locking key can be published in a newspaper, a problem Diffie and Hellman had posed but not solved. Adleman is about to become the third name in the answer.
suggested_refs: Diffie and Hellman, 'New Directions in Cryptography', IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, November 1976

stops.name: 545 Technology Square, the codes one through forty-two
stops.date_confidence: Pin inherited byte-identical from phil_zimmermann.journey.json and nick_szabo.journey.json; nick_szabo.report.md rules -71.0913 authoritative against a reported -71.0942. Collaboration and year attested; the count of forty-two broken candidates is reconstruction, carried by MacTutor, by Adleman himself in later interview, and by inventor-spotlight retellings, with no contemporaneous 1977 record. The research pool tagged the same figure attested in one place and reconstruction in another. Month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: Rivest and Shamir propose systems. Adleman breaks them. The division of labour is nobody's plan; he is the number theorist in the building, less interested in cryptography than in the mathematics underneath it, and he finds the flaw in each scheme faster than the other two can build the next. By the count all three give afterward there are forty-two of these, defeated at birthday parties and in corridors across a year. No document from 1977 records the number. The number is what they remember.
stops.quote: I was the number theorist in residence. Ron and Adi were really more interested in public crypto than I was initially.
stops.quote_source: CSO Online, 'Q&A: RSA crypto pioneer Adleman keeps pushing the limits'
suggested_refs: MIT Laboratory for Computer Science, 545 Technology Square, Cambridge; the building where the forty-two failed candidates were proposed and broken
sources: phil_zimmermann.journey.json, stop '545 Technology Square, the trapdoor before the tool'

stops.name: 545 Technology Square, the telephone call after the seder
stops.date_confidence: Date and pin inherited byte-identical from phil_zimmermann.journey.json, which dates the night after the Passover seder to 1977-04-02. Adleman's own account in CSO Online gives the dinner, the wine and the midnight telephone call without a calendar date.
stops.campa: Rivest goes to a Passover dinner, drinks a good deal of wine, and cannot sleep. Around midnight he telephones Adleman with a scheme built on the difficulty of factoring the product of two large primes. Adleman, who has broken forty-two systems in a year, does not break this one. He congratulates him on the telephone, inside the same call, before hanging up. Nobody can prove the thing unbreakable; he simply cannot see the flaw, and his failing to see it is the entire test the method has to pass.
stops.quote: Basically, Ron and Adi would propose many different solutions [42 to be exact], and I would quickly shoot them down. They would make many attempts over the months, and I would run into them at birthday parties and celebrations and find flaws. One night, at a Passover dinner, Ron drank a lot of wine. After dinner, around midnight, Ron called me and told me about the large prime number and factoring idea that would eventually become RSA. And right on the phone I said, 'Congratulations, you've done it!' I knew we couldn't prove it was unbreakable, but I couldn't see any flaws.
stops.quote_source: CSO Online, 'Q&A: RSA crypto pioneer Adleman keeps pushing the limits'
suggested_refs: The MIT Laboratory for Computer Science technical memorandum of April 1977, first written statement of the RSA method
sources: phil_zimmermann.journey.json, stop '545 Technology Square, the trapdoor before the tool'

stops.name: MIT, the third author
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor preserves both of Adleman's statements without dates. Placement in the weeks after the April breakthrough and before the December patent filing is inference, and the month is a default.
stops.campa: Rivest and Shamir put his name on the paper. Adleman tells them to take it off, on the grounds that the work is theirs. Then he reasons it through out loud: the paper will be the least important he is ever on, he will need lines on a vita for tenure, and he did after all do the intellectual labour of breaking codes one through forty-two. So he asks to be third. Alphabetical order does the rest, and the method is called RSA rather than RS because a man argued himself down to the last position on his own byline.
stops.quote: Take my name off the paper. It's your work
stops.quote_source: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Leonard Adleman', on the offer of co-authorship
suggested_refs: MacTutor's extended account of Adleman's reasoning toward third authorship, the origin of the letter A in RSA

stops.name: 545 Technology Square, the challenge printed in Scientific American
stops.date_confidence: Column and month attested (Scientific American, August 1977, Martin Gardner's 'Mathematical Games'). Pin inherited byte-identical. The research pool described the RSA-129 cryptogram as signed by the three authors; it was encrypted and posed by them, and a digital signature is a different operation.
stops.campa: Martin Gardner gives his Mathematical Games column over to the new cipher and prints a message encrypted under a 129-digit modulus, with a hundred dollars for whoever reads it. He tells his readers it would take millions of years. Requests for the technical memorandum arrive by the thousand, and the National Security Agency takes an interest that will occupy the next decade. A puzzle column puts a working public-key cipher in front of a general readership before the journals have it.
suggested_refs: Martin Gardner, 'Mathematical Games', Scientific American, August 1977, carrying the RSA-129 challenge cryptogram
sources: Scientific American, August 1977, cited in multiple histories of RSA

stops.name: Arlington, the address on the patent
stops.date_confidence: Filing date and residence attested on the face of US Patent 4,405,829 (cr.yp.to patent archive). The pin is the town; the patent's reachable copy gives no street address.
stops.campa: The application that becomes US Patent 4,405,829 is filed on the fourteenth of December with three home towns on it: Rivest of Belmont, Shamir of Cambridge, Adleman of Arlington. It is assigned to MIT and granted six years later. Licence terms, royalties and the question of who may use this arithmetic all descend from the document, and so does the quarrel that will put Phil Zimmermann under federal criminal investigation fifteen years later for giving the same arithmetic away.
suggested_refs: US Patent 4,405,829, 'Cryptographic communications system and method', filed 14 December 1977, granted 20 September 1983, assigned to MIT

stops.name: Cambridge, the method in Communications of the ACM
stops.date_confidence: Publication month and journal attested (Communications of the ACM, February 1978). Pin inherited byte-identical.
stops.campa: A Method for Obtaining Digital Signatures and Public-Key Cryptosystems appears in print. It runs to a few pages of number theory and carries three surnames in alphabetical order. Ralph Merkle's own paper, held three years by a referee who found it outside the main stream, runs in the same journal two months later and states that Rivest, Shamir and Adleman have also proposed a public key cryptosystem. Nick Szabo and Hal Finney will each build on this function decades later, and each will cite this issue.
suggested_refs: Rivest, Shamir and Adleman, 'A Method for Obtaining Digital Signatures and Public-Key Cryptosystems', Communications of the ACM 21(2), February 1978

segments.name: Los Angeles: the Chair, the Company, the Word

stops.name: USC, the move west
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (Wikipedia; MacTutor; USC Viterbi faculty page); month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: Adleman leaves MIT for the University of Southern California as a tenured associate professor of computer science. He is thirty-four. He will not move again: full professor in 1983, the Henry Salvatori Chair in 1985, a joint appointment in molecular biology afterward, and the same campus underfoot for the next forty-six years. The cipher he helped to test stays behind in Massachusetts as a patent held by MIT, and follows him to California as a company.
suggested_refs: USC Viterbi School of Engineering faculty page for Leonard Adleman
sources: USC Viterbi School of Engineering faculty page

stops.name: Redwood City, the company in an apartment
stops.date_confidence: Pin inherited byte-identical from hellman.journey.json and phil_zimmermann.journey.json. Founding year 1982 per Wikipedia 'RSA Security', FundingUniverse and RSA's own corporate history; the research pool's 1983 is not carried. The firm began in Adleman's apartment, so the Marine Parkway headquarters address of the 1990s is anachronistic here. MacTutor alone says Adleman was made president, which is reconstruction: Jim Bidzos joined on 1 February 1986 and was president and chief executive from 1986 to 1999. Month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: The three authors incorporate RSA Data Security to license what MIT holds the patent on. It begins in an apartment. MacTutor says Adleman served as its president and no second source says so; what is certain is that he stays an academic and lets the company be a company. Martin Hellman's journey records that the firm's own founding paper credits Diffie, Hellman and Merkle with inventing public key cryptography, and records too that Hellman was angry for years about the patents before crediting Jim Bidzos with building an industry.
suggested_refs: FundingUniverse company history of RSA Security Inc.; RSA Laboratories documents giving the later 100 Marine Parkway address

stops.name: USC, the primality test with Pomerance and Rumely
stops.date_confidence: Publication year attested (Annals of Mathematics, 1983; MacTutor; Wikipedia). Month and day are defaults. The Annals paper itself was not opened in this research and is known through summaries.
stops.campa: With Carl Pomerance and Robert Rumely he publishes in the Annals of Mathematics a method for deciding whether a number is prime, and the test carries the three surnames afterward. It answers the question standing directly behind RSA: the cipher needs large primes, and somebody has to certify that a candidate is one. He is made full professor the same year. The pure number theory and the commercial cipher are one subject seen from two angles, and he is working both ends of it.
suggested_refs: Adleman, Pomerance and Rumely, 'On distinguishing prime numbers from composite numbers', Annals of Mathematics, 1983

stops.name: Los Angeles, the singles dance
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. MacTutor is the sole source for the meeting and the six-week courtship, no independent corroboration was found, and MacTutor names neither the city nor the venue. The research pool's chronology lens tagged this attested and supplied Los Angeles, which the source does not support; its geography lens tags the same episode reconstruction and is right. The city-centre pin is a placeholder and the month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: He goes to a singles dance and meets Lori Bruce. They marry about six weeks later. One biography carries the story and nothing else does; the venue is unnamed, the city is unnamed, the month is unknown. It sits in the record beside a primality test and the founding of a company, dated only to the same year, and it is kept here on those terms: an episode with a shape and no coordinates, inside a life otherwise documented down to the town on a patent application.
suggested_refs: MacTutor's account of the singles dance and the six-week courtship, uncorroborated elsewhere

stops.name: USC, the seminar and the naming of the virus
stops.date_confidence: Date attested by Fred Cohen's own account in 'Computer Viruses: Theory and Experiments': conception 3 November 1983, demonstration 10 November 1983, at his weekly computer security seminar as a USC graduate student under Adleman. The research pool placed the demonstration at Lehigh University, which is a conflation with Cohen's later affiliation and with the unrelated 1987 Lehigh virus. The building is not identified in sources; the pin is the campus.
stops.campa: Fred Cohen, Adleman's graduate student, brings a program to his weekly security seminar and turns it loose on a VAX 11/750. It takes control of the machine in under thirty minutes by writing copies of itself into other programs. Adleman, who is at that moment reading molecular biology and thinking about how HIV enters a cell, supplies the word for what he is watching. He calls it a virus. The seminar ends and the machine is eventually scrapped. The word he supplies that afternoon is still the word.
stops.quote: I would meet with Fred on a regular basis to discuss this, and I at the same time was doing research on HIV in a molecular biology lab. So viruses and how they worked were sort of much in my mind and I was reading a lot about molecular biology at that time. And so somewhere along the line during our discussions I started calling these things computer viruses.
stops.quote_source: WeLiveSecurity (ESET), 'Professor Len Adleman explains how he coined the term computer virus', 2017
suggested_refs: Fred Cohen, 'Computer Viruses: Theory and Experiments' (all.net), giving 3 and 10 November 1983 and the VAX 11/750 demonstration
sources: Fred Cohen, 'Computer Viruses: Theory and Experiments'
USC Viterbi, 'Computer Virus: An Origin Story'

stops.name: USC, the student's paper goes out
stops.date_confidence: Publication year attested; Cohen's paper was presented at the 1984 IFIP security conference. Month and day are defaults. The secondary sources placing this at Lehigh University are not followed here.
stops.campa: Cohen's Computer Viruses: Theory and Experiments goes out under Adleman's supervision, with formal definitions and the demonstration written up. Adleman is asked about it at a cryptography conference by a Los Angeles Times reporter and answers that he has a student researching something they are calling computer viruses, that the research is embryonic, and that there is not much there yet. The word is loose in a newspaper before there is anything for it to describe outside one seminar room.
stops.quote: not much, I've got a student who is researching something we're calling computer viruses, but the research is embryotic and we haven't got much now
stops.quote_source: WeLiveSecurity (ESET), Adleman recounting what he told Los Angeles Times reporter Lee Dembart
suggested_refs: Fred Cohen, 'Computer Viruses: Theory and Experiments', presented at the 1984 IFIP security conference

stops.name: USC, the Henry Salvatori Chair
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (USC Viterbi faculty page); month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: He is appointed to the Henry Salvatori Chair in Computer Science, later elevated to Henry Salvatori Distinguished Professor, and holds the title for four decades. It is the last promotion that means anything in the ordinary sense. Everything after it is a change of subject rather than a change of rank: an immunology problem taken up in his forties, then a wet bench, then a test tube with a graph dissolved in water. The chair funds a computer scientist and gets, inside ten years, a molecular biologist who has founded a field.
suggested_refs: USC Viterbi School of Engineering, Henry Salvatori Chair in Computer Science
sources: USC Viterbi School of Engineering faculty page

segments.name: The Immune System and the Wet Bench

stops.name: UCSF Parnassus, the CD4 count as a control problem
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The Stanford CS course profile is the only source for the shape and dating of the Wofsy collaboration and it gives no year; the research pool's c.1986-1990 is inference, and 1988 is a placeholder inside that window. The joint publication is separately attested to 1993.
stops.campa: With David Wofsy at the University of California, San Francisco, Adleman treats the collapse of CD4 cells in AIDS as a failure of homeostatic regulation rather than as simple killing: a control system losing its setpoint. The mathematics is not the hard part. Getting HIV researchers to sit still for it is. He is a cryptographer with a theory about immunology and no standing in the room, and the wall he meets here is the reason he does the next thing he does.
suggested_refs: Stanford CS course profile, 'Leonard Adleman: The Father of DNA Computing'
sources: Stanford CS course profile, 'Leonard Adleman: The Father of DNA Computing'

stops.name: USC, learning the bench
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The Stanford CS course profile dates the wet-lab immersion to roughly 1990-1993 without a source; 1991 is a placeholder inside that window. Open contradiction, flagged and not resolved: Adleman's own account of coining the term 'computer virus' in 1983 depends on his already being in a molecular biology lab then. Both statements cannot be exactly right and neither is firm enough to correct the other.
stops.campa: To be heard by biologists he decides he has to speak as one, and goes into a laboratory at USC to learn technique from the beginning: pipettes, gels, enzymes, the whole apparatus of doing things to matter. Watson's Molecular Biology of the Gene is at his elbow. Twenty years earlier he had walked out of a physics course at San Francisco State because he did not like doing experiments. He is now in his forties and doing them, clumsily at first, in order to win an argument.
stops.quote: It came to me because of my interest in theoretical computer science and HIV. My interest in HIV led me to ask a colleague if I could get into his lab to become more proficient in professional molecular biology. There I saw the world of DNA. It was like being in Disney World!
stops.quote_source: CSO Online, 'Q&A: RSA crypto pioneer Adleman keeps pushing the limits'
suggested_refs: James Watson, Molecular Biology of the Gene, named by Adleman as the book behind the immersion
sources: Stanford CS course profile, 'Leonard Adleman: The Father of DNA Computing'

stops.name: Los Angeles, an unnamed college and the slides for Sneakers
stops.date_confidence: Release year of the film attested; month and day are defaults. Adleman's own account on the USC Laboratory for Molecular Science 'Sneakers' page says the scene was shot at a small college in Los Angeles, which no source names, so the city-centre pin is a placeholder. The research pool's Universal Studios location is unsupported and is not carried, and its description of the on-screen slides as computer graphics inverts what Adleman says happened.
stops.campa: A film about a team that steals a codebreaking box needs a lecture scene no mathematician will laugh at, and Adleman writes it. He makes the slides himself on a Macintosh; the production has them redrawn by hand, because hand-drawn looks more realistic on camera. He gives the character Gunter Janek the line about a breakthrough of Gaussian proportions, putting Carl Friedrich Gauss into a Robert Redford picture by way of a USC office.
suggested_refs: USC Laboratory for Molecular Science, 'Sneakers' page, Adleman's own account of preparing the slides
sources: USC Laboratory for Molecular Science 'Sneakers' page

stops.name: Los Angeles, the immunology paper
stops.date_confidence: Year and journal attested through MacTutor. The paper's title, volume and pagination were not obtained in this research and the journal text was not opened. Month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: The work with Wofsy reaches print in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. It is the only medical paper on the vita of a man who will be given the Turing Award, and no source reached in this research gives its title, volume or pagination. Without the immunology he has no reason to enter a laboratory, and without the laboratory he never meets the enzyme that hands him the next idea. The argument he could not win by talking he has now made in the literature of the people he wanted to convince.
suggested_refs: Adleman and Wofsy, Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes, 1993; full citation not obtained in this research

stops.name: USC, the textbook in bed and Turing's 1936 paper
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to date. MacTutor preserves Adleman's account of the insight arriving while he was ill in bed with a molecular biology textbook and gives no date; placement in the months before the 1994 experiment is inference and the month is a default.
stops.campa: Ill in bed with a molecular biology textbook, he reads the description of DNA polymerase moving along a strand, reading one base and writing another, and he recognises it. Alan Turing had described that machine in 1936 as an abstraction, a head on a tape. The enzyme is the head and the tape at once, inside a cell, doing it several billion times over in every living thing. Computation is easy, he concludes, and the components are all around us, and one of them is already inside him.
stops.quote: While lying there admiring this amazing enzyme, I was struck by its similarity to something described in 1936 by Alan Turing
suggested_refs: Alan Turing, 'On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem', 1936, named by Adleman as the text the enzyme reminded him of

stops.name: USC, the seven cities in a test tube
stops.date_confidence: Experiment year attested; the month is inference from the November publication and is a default. The Laboratory for Molecular Science pin is the campus location given in the research pool, not a documented room.
stops.campa: He encodes a seven-node directed graph as short strands of DNA, one sequence for each city, one for each road, and pours them together. The strands anneal into paths. Then he spends a week with PCR and affinity purification throwing away every path that is not a Hamiltonian one: every route that misses a city or enters one twice. The computation itself takes about a second in a common test tube. Reading the answer back out takes seven days, which is the part nobody quotes.
stops.quote: I took a pinch (about 10^14 molecules) of each of the different sequences and put them into a common test tube... Within about one second, I had the answer.
suggested_refs: USC Laboratory for Molecular Science, site of the 1994 Hamiltonian path experiment

stops.name: Los Angeles, Science volume 266
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the issue date: Science vol. 266, pp. 1021-1024, 11 November 1994.
stops.campa: Molecular Computation of Solutions to Combinatorial Problems runs to four pages in Science and starts a field. The instance is trivial; a child with a pencil beats the test tube. What it demonstrates is that the substrate is arbitrary. Silicon is a convenience and not a requirement, and a hard problem can be set on a bucket of molecules working all at once. Adleman is called the father of DNA computing from this paper onward, and does not dispute the title.
stops.quote: This experiment demonstrates the feasibility of carrying out computations at the molecular level.
stops.quote_source: Adleman, 'Molecular Computation of Solutions to Combinatorial Problems', Science 266, 11 November 1994
suggested_refs: Adleman, 'Molecular Computation of Solutions to Combinatorial Problems', Science 266:1021-1024, 11 November 1994

stops.name: 545 Technology Square, the magic words
stops.date_confidence: The RSA-129 factorization was completed and announced in April 1994; the day is given as 26 April in several accounts and is carried with that caveat. The pin is the challenge's origin, inherited byte-identical, not the location of the distributed effort, which had none.
stops.campa: Derek Atkins, Michael Graff, Arjen Lenstra and Paul Leyland finish factoring the 129-digit number Gardner printed in 1977, using six hundred volunteers and idle machines across the early internet. Millions of years turns out to be seventeen. The plaintext reads THE MAGIC WORDS ARE SQUEAMISH OSSIFRAGE. In the same year the third author of that challenge is in a laboratory in Los Angeles proving that a test tube can compute, which is one of the two directions this arithmetic can be attacked from.
suggested_refs: Accounts of the RSA Factoring Challenge and the 1994 factorization of RSA-129
sources: Cryptography histories of the RSA Factoring Challenge

stops.name: Redwood City, the company sold
stops.date_confidence: Acquisition by Security Dynamics attested for 1996; contradiction flagged and not resolved on two axes. FundingUniverse dates it to April 1996 and values it at four million Security Dynamics shares, approximately 251 million dollars; Wikipedia dates it to July 1996; MacTutor gives a flat 200 million. April is carried as the earlier of the two dates, with the day a default. Pin inherited byte-identical.
stops.campa: Security Dynamics buys RSA Data Security in a stock deal. The figure is reported at two hundred million dollars in one account and about two hundred and fifty-one million in another, and the month is April in one and July in another; the disagreement is kept here rather than averaged away. Fourteen years earlier the company was an apartment. What is being bought is the exclusive right to license a page of arithmetic three academics wrote down in Cambridge.

stops.name: New York, the Kanellakis Award to six men
stops.date_confidence: Award year and the six joint recipients attested by ACM records; the award was presented in March 1997, and the month and day here are defaults for the award year. Pin is the atlas's canonical New York station, inherited byte-identical from hellman.journey.json and ralph_merkle.journey.json; the banquet venue is not confirmed in any source consulted. stops.campa: The ACM's new Paris Kanellakis Theory and Practice Award goes to six men at once for public-key cryptography: Adleman, Whitfield Diffie, Martin Hellman, Ralph Merkle, Ronald Rivest, Adi Shamir.
